ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Lewy bodies are intraneuronal aggregates of alpha‑synuclein that destroy dopaminergic neurons, causing Parkinsonian motor symptoms and dementia. They spread from brainstem to cortex in a predictable pattern.

sections.p: Lewy bodies are eosinophilic inclusions in neurons, composed of alpha‑synuclein filaments. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by imaging and post‑mortem confirmation.
b: Eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions with dense core and pale halo

t.b: Shows reduced dopamine transporter uptake in basal ganglia, confirming dopaminergic loss
Excludes structural lesions; may show cortical atrophy in advanced stages
Low levels suggest Lewy body pathology, but not routinely used

sections.p: The Braak staging system describes progression from brainstem (stage I) to neocortex (stage VI). Clinical severity correlates with stage and symptom burden.
b: Stage I–II: autonomic and REM sleep changes
Stage V–VI: dementia and cortical dysfunction

sections.p: Lewy body disease is idiopathic but linked to age, genetics (SNCA, LRRK2), and environmental toxins. In low‑resource settings, infections like HIV or malaria may exacerbate neurodegeneration.

t.b: Identifies SNCA or LRRK2 mutations; informs prognosis
High load may worsen neurocognitive decline

sections.p: Patients show fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, and classic Parkinsonism. Autonomic dysfunction (orthostatic hypotension) is common.
Tests confirm dopaminergic loss, rule out mimics, and assess complications. Availability may be limited; clinical criteria can guide management.

t.b: Normal MRI supports Lewy body disease

sections.p: Rapid cognitive decline, severe autonomic failure, or sudden falls may signal advanced disease or superimposed infections.
Treat underlying causes, use dopaminergic therapy, and manage non‑motor symptoms. Avoid drugs that worsen hallucinations or autonomic instability.
Regular monitoring of motor scores, cognition, and autonomic function. Early detection of infections and vaccination reduce complications.
b: Blood pressure monitoring for orthostatic changes

sections.p: Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy, and drug‑induced parkinsonism.
b: MSA – autonomic failure precedes motor signs

sections.p: Normal DAT scan in early disease; CSF alpha‑synuclein may be low in other synucleinopathies.

faq.q: Can Lewy bodies be treated directly?
faq.a: No, treatment targets symptoms and underlying neurodegeneration, not the aggregates themselves.

faq.q: Do all Parkinsonian patients have Lewy bodies?
faq.a: No, only about 70% of Parkinson disease cases show Lewy bodies; others have different pathology.
Currently, no cure exists; management focuses on symptom control and quality of life.
